Two new EEG recordings: what repeats after the markers?

Subject 029, session 2 · 29ByBP | Subject 030 · 30ByANT

Subject 030 has a repeatable postmarker voltage change, but a clean canonical N2–P2 pair is not established. In both 30-event blocks, Cz becomes more negative relative to the recorded CPz reference, with a broad trough around 0.55–0.63 s after the corrected onset. Subject 029’s second session again shows only small, uncertain Cz changes. Large frontal signals, reference dependence and unknown event-code meanings limit a pain-specific interpretation.

These are two participants from different datasets, not two participants from 30ByANT. Session 1 and session 2 of subject 029 are repeated recordings of one participant. No cross-subject or cross-dataset statistical comparison is made.

030 · 30ByANT2,491.547 s; 32 channels30 s22 events and 30 s32 events, separatelyMarker −100 ms; recorded CPz reference

The 30ByANT README reports a 100 ms delay in laser markers, so analysis onset is set 100 samples earlier at 1,000 Hz. Thus an event 200 ms after the stored marker is 300 ms after the estimated laser onset. This correction is applied only to 30ByANT. Physical timing for 29ByBP remains unconfirmed.

The README describes 30 trials per participant, but this uploaded 30ByANT file contains two separated 30-event blocks. The six isolated markers s11, s12, s8, s9, s13 and s14 between those blocks are excluded from the repeated-event analysis. The meanings of s22 and s32 remain unverified because the event-code dictionary was not supplied or retrievable. Neither block is labelled here as a particular treatment, energy, pain level, or confirmed laser condition. The supplied event tables contain no pain ratings.

1. Cz changes in the conventional search windows

Trials are aligned, then each channel’s mean from −500 to 0 ms is subtracted. Primary averages include every selected trial. The table shows means in 150–300 ms and 300–500 ms after analysis onset with 0.1–30 Hz filtering. These windows provide a consistent check against the earlier analysis; naming a window “N” or “P” does not identify a component.

Recording / block150–300 ms mean, µV95% CI300–500 ms mean, µV95% CI
029 session 2-0.32[-0.99, 0.31]-0.52[-1.44, 0.30]
030 s22-0.10[-1.59, 1.48]-3.62[-5.80, -1.55]
030 s32-3.07[-4.89, -1.19]-7.15[-9.16, -5.19]

Both s22 and s32 are negative in the later window, rather than showing the expected positive P2 relative to CPz. The later-window mean remains negative in odd and even trials and differs from the nonstimulus comparison in both blocks using the uncorrected trial-bootstrap intervals. Subject 029 session 2’s two direct baseline-relative window intervals include zero.

The broad Cz minimum in an exploratory 300–800 ms window is −6.10 µV at 625 ms for s22 and −9.36 µV at 555 ms for s32. These are descriptive troughs in an average, not confirmed N2 latencies. Their amplitudes should not be used to claim greater pain in s32: block meanings, ratings, recording state and possible order effects are unknown.

The same later negativity is present without added filtering and with a 30 Hz low-pass: s22’s 300–500 ms mean is −5.16 µV stored, −5.17 µV low-pass and −3.62 µV band-pass; s32’s is −7.68, −7.68 and −7.15 µV, respectively. Mild filtering smooths the traces and changes slow offsets but does not create the overall negative shift.

2. Why reference choice and artifacts matter

EEG records voltage differences. For the supplementary mean-mastoid view, Cz is transformed as Cz_new = Cz_recorded − (M1_recorded + M2_recorded)/2. The physical CPz reference contribution cancels algebraically. This does not make M1/M2 electrically neutral or remove their artifacts.

After that change, the 300–500 ms Cz means become +27.02 µV (s22) and +36.63 µV (s32). The earlier-window means are also positive (+12.93 and +17.52 µV). The mastoid-referenced trace contains a strong slow trend, including prestimulus slope. Therefore a large positive deflection in this view is insufficient to identify a clean N2–P2 pair. The primary results retain the recorded CPz reference, and the alternative is explicitly a sensitivity check rather than a selected “better-looking” result.

Subject 030 has no separately labelled EOG channels. Fp1/Fp2/Fpz can flag large frontal signals but cannot establish ocular origin. The median Fp1 peak-to-peak amplitude over −0.5 to +1 s is approximately 161 µV in s22 and 400 µV in s32, compared with about 20 and 26 µV at Cz. Eye movements, blinks, muscle activity or task-related behavior are plausible contributors; no particular source is proven. No ICA, regression or source localization was used.

A coarse sensitivity screen retains 18/30 s22 trials, 6/30 s32 trials and 74/75 BP session 2 trials. It requires ≤150 µV peak-to-peak in selected central channels and ≤200 µV in frontal channels for ANT or VEO/HEOR for BP, over −0.5 to +1 s. The ANT later-window Cz means remain negative in the retained sets (−4.23 and −7.74 µV), but only six retained s32 trials make this a weak quality check. The screen can reject real responses and does not certify clean trials.

3. Spectral patterns to follow up

These are exploratory total-power changes from −1.00 to −0.25 s versus +0.25 to +1.00 s, measured on the stored signal. Alpha is 8–13 Hz and beta is 13–30 Hz. Posterior power is averaged over O1, Oz, O2 and POz before computing each trial’s post/pre dB ratio. Negative dB means lower postevent power.

The clearest candidates are lower beta power in s22, particularly posteriorly, and lower alpha power in s32. Their all-trial directions agree in odd/even splits. Posterior s22 beta remains about −1.61 dB in the screened subset; s32 alpha decreases become smaller in its six retained trials. These intervals are uncorrected across several measures. Artifact contamination, short analysis windows and block differences mean these are leads for replication, not established pain biomarkers. Subject 029 session 2 has no clear direct post/pre alpha or beta change in these selected regions.

4. Subject 029 session 2 compared with session 1

Cz remains small and uncertain: session 1’s early/later means were −0.23/−0.38 µV; session 2’s are −0.32/−0.52 µV. A stable canonical N2–P2 pair is not established in either session with the supplied header mapping and marker times.

Late 700–1,500 ms shifts repeat in the channels labelled VEO and HEOR. Their session 2 means are −13.22 and −13.42 µV, versus approximately −11.63 and −12.76 µV in session 1. This is stronger evidence for a repeatable event-related ocular-channel pattern than for a Cz N2–P2. It does not identify a cortical source or pain intensity. Session 2’s Fp2 late mean is also large (−29.02 µV).

As in session 1, BP’s header specifies 63 channels while its sidecar lists 64 in a different order. Header-only names include VEO and HEOR; sidecar-only names include IO, FT9 and FT10. Analysis follows the binary header, so anatomical interpretations remain conditional on its accuracy. ANT’s 32 channel names and order match across header and sidecar.

Methods, reproducibility and interpretation limits

Both recordings are sampled at 1,000 Hz. BP is decoded as multiplexed little-endian signed 16-bit values, scaled by 0.1 µV/count. ANT is multiplexed little-endian IEEE 32-bit float, with header resolution 1 µV and microvolt units corroborated by the sidecar. All decoded samples are finite, and binary sizes divide into complete channel frames. All stimulus event-table indices match the marker file after converting its one-based positions to zero-based indices. Browser-added “(1)” suffixes are handled by explicit recording-prefix selection; source files are unchanged.

Continuous data are filtered before extracting −1 to +2 s epochs, using SciPy’s order-2 Butterworth band-pass design at 0.1–30 Hz in second-order sections with forward/backward application. The resulting band-pass has four poles per pass and a squared magnitude response after forward/backward application. A separate 30 Hz low-pass-only check is performed at Cz. No extra notch, resampling, ICA or interpolation is used. Zero-phase filtering can smear transients; exact response onset is not inferred from the first visible change. “Stored” means no added filter, not proof that acquisition or export filters were absent. BP’s header filter table and JSON disagree about the availability of software-filter information.

The nonstimulus comparison uses epochs centered 5 s before each analyzed onset, with the same local baseline. These are not sham stimulation trials and may include unmarked task behavior. Spectral estimates use 500-sample Hann Welch segments, 250-sample overlap, constant detrending and 2 Hz bins; all bins falling within each stated band are included. Total power mixes evoked and non-phase-locked activity. No exact-onset claim is made from these broad power windows.

Confidence intervals use 2,000 trial-bootstrap resamples with fixed seeds, assume exchangeable trials, and are within-recording, uncorrected intervals. Plot bands are pointwise, not simultaneous confidence bands. Odd/even splits assess descriptive repeatability, not independent-population validation. The broad trough window and reference check are exploratory. No statistical test of the s22–s32 difference, no subject-level generalization and no classifier are claimed.

Laser-evoked N2/P2 waves can reflect attention and salience as well as nociceptive processing; they do not alone time subjective pain onset or quantify pain intensity. See Lee et al. (2009) and Iannetti et al. (2008). Here the missing event-code meanings and large reference/artifact effects are the immediate limitations.

Next useful evidence

Obtain task-30ByANT_events.json to identify s22/s32 and the six intervening markers, plus per-trial ratings if available. Confirm the BP code definitions and channel mapping. Then inspect artifacts trial by trial, predefine the desired montage and windows, and validate any voltage or power pattern in another participant from the same dataset. The present data support an event-related change in subject 030; they do not yet support calling it a pain-specific N2–P2 response.

Re-run

python analyze_uploads.py /path/to/uploaded-files
python reference_and_comparison.py
python build_report.py

Dependencies: Python, NumPy, SciPy, pandas and Matplotlib. Input folders must contain exactly one matching file per required suffix for each named recording. The bundle includes scripts, per-trial TSVs, summary JSON, input hashes, figures and this report. Large derived caches are regenerated by the first script. The earlier session 1 Cz average and summary are included as derived comparison data; the script uses that average when the earlier cache is unavailable. Trial TSV N/P fields and summary extrema are numerical window measurements, not validated component detections.
